paragraphs: I was allowed to study abroad for three months at the hospital attached to the Medical University of Vienna, a very large university with 600 students per year. It is a very internationally flavored university where many students are enrolled, not only from within Austria but from other European countries. As befits a city that was ranked number one in the world's most livable city ranking, Vienna was a very beautiful and safe city. Public transportation was well developed, and I never had trouble getting anywhere. Supermarkets are all closed on Sundays and even on weekdays close at 19:30, which was a little hard. Prices are about the same as in Japan, but eating out is more expensive than in Japan.

After it was decided that I would study in Vienna, what worried me most was that the first language in Austria is German. When I actually went, as I had heard that medical personnel can speak English, almost everyone spoke English fluently. Including other European countries, a great deal of effort is put into English education, and even small children are fluent in English, and I keenly felt the difference from Japan.

Also, when I said I was from Japan in my self-introduction, people were very curious, saying "Where in Japan?", "I know Nagoya!", "I'm thinking of traveling to Japan sometime!", and I felt that everyone has a good image of Japan. I was also asked many times about Japan's healthcare system and medical situation, and I exchanged opinions on it and was able to spend very fulfilling days.

I rotated through obstetrics and gynecology, pediatric cardiology and radiology, one month each. In every department I was taught in English and was blessed with enthusiastic doctors, and I was able to spend a fulfilling three months. Among the sixth-year students, some actually work at the attached hospital and receive a salary, and when they were in the same department I did rounds with them and observed first visits, and I was stimulated every day by their excellence.

In obstetrics and gynecology, after taking part in the morning conference, I observed surgery or outpatient clinics. There was no fixed schedule and a high degree of freedom, but for that reason I had to say what I wanted to do and what I was interested in, so there was a hardship different from Japan. If you assert nothing, the day just passes with nothing. Thinking every day about which operation to watch and which outpatient clinic to go to, I learned the importance of moving actively and had an irreplaceable experience. During surgical observation I was allowed into the surgical field and to do simple procedures, which was very educational. Because the physiques of Japanese and Westerners are completely different, even small things such as pregnant women's bellies being less noticeable than those of Japanese women were fresh.

Pediatric cardiology is a small subdivided department within pediatrics, so I was able to spend a month homelike with about five doctors. Because there were few people, they took very good care of me in the clerkship, reading ECGs together and discussing, and sometimes letting me examine patients, which was very educational. Since local students were doing their clerkship in this pediatric cardiology department, I was also able to interact with them, and they spoke to me casually and became friends with me. It was an experience unique to study abroad and I enjoyed it very much. Because I did rounds with the students on the same ward every day, I even felt sad to part with the hospitalized children.

Radiology consisted of about 20 doctors, each reading their assigned examinations such as MRI, CT and X-ray. Every day I chose what I wanted to see, followed a doctor, and was given explanations in English while observing the reading. Among them, what impressed me most was fetal MRI, in which they put great effort and I was able to see several fetal MRIs every day. I think the appeal of clerkships abroad is being able to see things one cannot see much in Japan, so it was a very good experience.

I am sincerely grateful to everyone who supported this study abroad: Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office, the staff of the Academic Affairs Division, my seniors, my family and the people of the Medical University of Vienna, who gave me this very valuable opportunity. Thank you very much.
